principle_name: Never Say Sell — Grow Existing Client Relationships by Asking How You Can Be More Helpful
author: Tom McMakin & Jacob Parks
when_to_use: As the foundational mindset for every MOTM BD interaction — especially when talking to existing clients or warm prospects about expanding the engagement. The shift from asking how can I sell you more to asking how can I help you more changes everything about the conversation.
when_not_to_use: This is not a reason to avoid ever asking for business directly — the Ask is still essential. It is a mindset that governs how the BD conversation is framed before the ask.
principle: Expert services are not sold the way products are sold. Clients buy expertise on the basis of reputation, referral, and relationship — not features and price. The word sell is associated with manipulation, information asymmetry, and self-interest. The word help is associated with service, expertise, and partnership. The most effective BD professionals in expert services never think about selling. They think about helping — and the work follows from that. Walt Shill of Accenture put it plainly: We are the ambulance. We have a moral obligation to use our skills to solve problems. Expertise that goes unused is a failure.
questions_to_ask: Based on what we have done together so far, where do you see the biggest gaps in your sales execution that we have not yet addressed?
If there was one thing we could add to what we currently do for you that would have the biggest impact on your pipeline, what would it be?
Who else in your organisation is dealing with a sales challenge that you think MOTM could help with?
recommended_action: Reframe every BD conversation with an existing client around how MOTM can be more helpful — not how MOTM can sell more. Ask questions before proposing. Listen for unmet needs before presenting solutions. The expansion of the MOTM engagement should feel to the client like a natural response to their expressed needs — not like a sales pitch.
what_not_to_do: Do not open an existing client conversation with a capability presentation or a proposal for additional services. Do not position expansion as upselling — position it as helping. Do not skip the listening stage to get to the pitch. Do not wait for the client to identify their own problems — bring insight about what you have observed.
motm_application: When a MOTM client is renewing, the BD conversation should not be here is what else we can do for you. It should be here is what we have observed about your sales situation and here are two or three areas where we think there is more we could help with. Would you like to explore any of those? This framing positions MOTM as a trusted advisor diagnosing needs — not a vendor trying to expand a contract.

principle_name: Farming Is More Valuable Than Hunting — 80-90% of Expert Services Growth Comes From Existing Clients
author: Tom McMakin & Jacob Parks
when_to_use: When prioritising where MOTM BD should invest its time and effort — and when an existing client relationship is underutilised but has potential for expansion.
when_not_to_use: Farming is not a reason to stop acquiring new clients entirely — it is a reason to ensure existing client relationships are being actively cultivated, not just serviced.
principle: Expert services firms report that 80% to 90% of new revenues come from expanding existing client relationships — not from winning new logos. Farming existing clients is cheaper, faster, lower risk, and higher probability than cold hunting for new business. It costs six to eight times more to win a new client than to grow an existing one. Yet most firms invest disproportionate effort in hunting while underinvesting in farming. Bloom where you are planted — the richest ground for new work is the client who already trusts you and knows the quality of what you deliver.
questions_to_ask: Which of our current MOTM clients have the most untapped potential for expanded engagement — and are we actively farming those relationships?
What percentage of our BD investment is going into existing clients versus hunting for new logos — and is that the right balance?
For each active MOTM engagement, what are the next one or two natural expansions of our work that we have not yet proposed?
recommended_action: Dedicate a structured portion of MOTM BD time to farming existing client relationships — account planning, proactive conversations about what else could help, bringing insight from other clients, and asking directly for introductions within the client organisation. Treat existing client growth as a formal BD activity, not as a by-product of good delivery.
what_not_to_do: Do not assume that good delivery will automatically generate expansion. Do not leave existing clients unattended between project milestones. Do not wait for the client to call with a new need — bring observations and ideas proactively. Do not treat existing client conversations as status updates — treat them as strategic BD conversations.
motm_application: MOTM should have an explicit account farming process for every active engagement. After 90 days of delivery, the BD person should review the engagement with fresh eyes: what else is happening in this client's sales organisation that MOTM could address? What other people in the company have sales challenges we have not yet spoken to? What expansion of scope would be the most natural next step based on what we have observed? These questions belong in a monthly account review, not left to chance.

principle_name: The Diamond of Opportunity — Six Distinct Ways to Grow Within an Existing Client
author: Tom McMakin & Jacob Parks
when_to_use: During account planning for any active MOTM client — to identify the specific growth opportunities available and prioritise which ones to pursue first.
when_not_to_use: Do not attempt INNOVATE or EVOLVE work before the foundational trust and credibility from excellent delivery has been established. Start at the base of the diamond and work upward.
principle: There are six distinct ways to grow work within an existing client. MORE: the same work for the same buyer — the easiest and most natural expansion. EXPAND: different work for the same buyer — adjacent services the buyer already trusts you to deliver. EXTEND: the same work for a different buyer — taking proven work to other parts of the client organisation. REACH: different work for a different buyer — expanding both the service and the relationship simultaneously. EVOLVE: new work with the same buyer — work you have not done before, earned through maximum trust. INNOVATE: new work with a new buyer — the most challenging, highest-risk expansion requiring both trust and credibility in new contexts. The base of the diamond (MORE) is always the right starting point. Most firms leave enormous value in the diamond untouched.
questions_to_ask: For our most active MOTM clients, where on the Diamond of Opportunity are we currently operating — and what is the most natural next step?
Who else in this client organisation could benefit from a similar MOTM engagement — and has our buyer introduced us to them?
What adjacent service to what we currently deliver would be the most natural EXPAND opportunity with our most trusting buyers?
recommended_action: Map every active MOTM client against the six diamond points. Identify the current position and the one or two most accessible next steps. Build a 6-12 month account plan for each major client that specifies which diamond points will be targeted, in what sequence, and who will lead each expansion conversation.
what_not_to_do: Do not try to jump to INNOVATE or REACH before earning the trust and credibility required. Do not present all six diamond opportunities to a client simultaneously — they will feel overwhelmed and the conversation will collapse. Do not assume the same buyer will champion every expansion — some require a different sponsor.
motm_application: A MOTM client who has been working with one SE in one territory represents the base of the diamond. MORE means adding a second SE or expanding the target account list. EXPAND means adding cold call coaching or email sequence development to the same buyer. EXTEND means introducing MOTM to the marketing head or the CEO of the same company for a different sales function. Each of these is a distinct expansion that must be planned, sequenced, and executed differently.

principle_name: The Five Challenges of Growing Within a Client — Why Expansion Does Not Happen Automatically
author: Tom McMakin & Jacob Parks
when_to_use: When diagnosing why an active MOTM client is not expanding — or when anticipating the barriers to expansion before they become obstacles.
when_not_to_use: These challenges are structural, not personal. Do not interpret slow expansion as a relationship failure — identify which specific challenge is operating and address it directly.
principle: Expert services firms consistently underestimate how hard expansion is. Five structural challenges block natural growth. 1) The client knows your current work but not your full capability — they have categorised you as the person who does X, not the person who could also do Y. 2) Internal complexity within the client firm — siloed buyers, competing champions, matrix organisations, and political dynamics all prevent referrals from happening. 3) Network complexity — two networks trying to interact (all of your firm's capabilities versus all of the client's buyers) creates overwhelming combinatorial complexity. 4) The difficulty of introducing colleagues — new experts must rebuild trust and credibility independently, weakening the transfer. 5) Scale — as both firms get bigger, bureaucracy and the Ringlemann Effect reduce urgency, coordination, and individual commitment. Understanding which challenge is operating in a specific client relationship is the first step to addressing it.
questions_to_ask: Does our buyer know the full range of what MOTM offers — or have they categorised us narrowly by what we do for them today?
Is there someone else in this client organisation who could benefit from MOTM but our buyer has not introduced us to — and if so, why not?
If we wanted to introduce a second MOTM person into this client, what would make that introduction work — and what would kill it?
recommended_action: For each major MOTM client, diagnose which of the five challenges is the primary barrier to expansion. If the barrier is narrow capability perception, proactively share what else MOTM does in adjacent areas. If the barrier is organisational complexity, ask the buyer directly to facilitate introductions. If the barrier is trust transfer, invest in meeting the new buyer in person before any capability conversation.
what_not_to_do: Do not assume expansion will happen naturally just because the buyer is happy with current work. Do not try to introduce a new MOTM person into a client without being present to facilitate the trust transfer personally. Do not allow the client to categorise MOTM permanently as the company that does one specific thing.
motm_application: If a MOTM client has been happily engaged for 12 months and has not expanded the relationship, the first question is which of the five challenges is operating. Is it that the MD does not know MOTM does more than the one thing they were hired for? Is it that the Sales Head who is the buyer does not want to refer MOTM to the Operations Head because of internal politics? Is it that the client organisation is large and siloed? Diagnosing correctly determines the intervention.

principle_name: Credibility Does Not Travel as Easily as Trust — Build Both Separately When Expanding
author: Tom McMakin & Jacob Parks
when_to_use: When introducing MOTM to a new buyer within an existing client — especially when that buyer has not worked directly with MOTM before and is in a different function or division than the current champion.
when_not_to_use: This distinction matters most for EXTEND, REACH, and INNOVATE work. For MORE work with the same buyer, trust and credibility are already established.
principle: Trust — confidence that someone has your best interests at heart — and credibility — confidence that someone can do the work — scale differently when moving across a client organisation. Trust travels somewhat through relationships: if a buyer vouches for MOTM, a colleague is more likely to extend provisional trust. But credibility must be independently established. A new buyer who does not know MOTM's work cannot evaluate it based on their colleague's recommendation alone. They need specific case studies, references, and evidence of capability that is relevant to their specific situation. Treating both trust and credibility as automatic when crossing to a new buyer is the most common cause of failed expansion conversations.
questions_to_ask: For this new buyer, what specific evidence of MOTM's credibility in their specific area would be most compelling?
What case study from another client most closely resembles what this new buyer needs — and can we lead with that?
How can our existing buyer facilitate a warm introduction that transfers some trust while we build credibility independently?
recommended_action: When moving to a new buyer within an existing client, plan the trust transfer and credibility building as two separate activities. Ask the existing buyer to make a warm introduction that frames MOTM in the context of a specific outcome they have experienced. Then immediately demonstrate credibility through a specific case study or insight relevant to the new buyer's situation — before any capability presentation.
what_not_to_do: Do not assume a warm referral from an existing buyer will do all the credibility work automatically. Do not show up to a new buyer with a general MOTM capability presentation — show up with a specific case study that mirrors their situation. Do not allow the new buyer to evaluate MOTM based solely on what they have heard from a colleague.
motm_application: When a MOTM client's Sales Head introduces MOTM to the MD for an expanded conversation, the meeting should open with a specific case study — not a general MOTM overview. The Sales Head's endorsement transfers some trust; MOTM must immediately demonstrate credibility that is relevant to what the MD cares about. The case study should feature a company similar to theirs, a challenge similar to what the MD faces, and a specific quantified outcome. This combination of transferred trust and demonstrated credibility is what converts expansion conversations.

principle_name: Discipline 1 — Do Good Work: Excellence Is the Prerequisite for Every Expansion Conversation
author: Tom McMakin & Jacob Parks
when_to_use: As the constant foundation for all MOTM account expansion. Before any expansion conversation is had, the question must be: are we WOWing this client with our current delivery?
when_not_to_use: Good work is necessary but not sufficient for expansion — it creates the foundation but expansion still requires proactive farming, asking, and introducing new capabilities. Do not rely on delivery quality alone.
principle: The simplest formula for winning expansion work is excellent delivery. Bill Green of Accenture built 150 clients that generated over $100M per year in fees — by bringing the absolute best of the firm to every engagement, consistently, over decades. Good work is the prerequisite for every expansion conversation. It is not the sales pitch — it is the right to be heard. The four levels of client satisfaction are: Good (met expectations), Excellent (exceeded expectations and clients recommend you), Lagniappe (gave extra value without being asked, demonstrating genuine investment in the client's success), and Pivot (strategic advice that helped the client achieve their underlying goals, not just their stated scope). Only Excellent and above reliably generate expansion opportunities.
questions_to_ask: Honestly, is our current delivery WOWing this client — or are we merely meeting expectations?
What is the one thing we could do this month that would give this client an unexpected extra value without being asked?
Are we tracking what this client says when they are asked about their experience with MOTM — or are we assuming they are satisfied?
recommended_action: Set a quarterly internal review for each MOTM client to honestly assess delivery quality against the four levels. Identify what would move current delivery from Good to Excellent or from Excellent to Lagniappe. Build one specific lagniappe into every client engagement — a proactive extra that demonstrates genuine investment in the client's success beyond the contracted scope.
what_not_to_do: Do not begin any expansion conversation with a client whose current delivery is at Good but not Excellent. Do not wait for a renewal conversation to assess delivery quality — review it continuously. Do not assume the absence of complaints means the client is delighted — most satisfied clients are merely satisfied, not advocates.
motm_application: Before any MOTM account expansion conversation, the BD person should be able to answer: Is this client WOWed by our current delivery? If the honest answer is no or probably, the priority is to fix delivery before expanding the conversation. The expansion conversation will fail if the client's experience of current delivery does not give them a strong emotional basis for trusting MOTM with more.

principle_name: Discipline 2 — Be a Good Friend: Invest in Client Relationships Beyond the Project Scope
author: Tom McMakin & Jacob Parks
chapter: Chapter 13 — Discipline 2: Be a Good Friend
when_to_use: Continuously throughout every active MOTM client engagement — not only at renewal time or when an expansion opportunity arises. The investment in the relationship must happen consistently for the relationship to be deep enough to support expansion.
when_not_to_use: Being a good friend does not mean ignoring professional boundaries or blurring the client-vendor relationship in ways that create confusion. It means genuine human investment in the person behind the business title.
principle: Fridge rights is the standard. Jacob's friend Riggs has earned the right to walk into Jacob's kitchen and help himself to a beer — because the relationship has that depth and trust. Expert services professionals who grow their work consistently are those who invest in relationships as if they were friendships: they remember what matters to their clients as people, they follow up on personal milestones, they buy the drinks, they show up in person when it matters, and they ask questions that are genuinely about the person, not just the project. Trust in expert services is built one human interaction at a time. Every act of genuine friendship is a deposit in the trust account that eventually makes expansion natural.
questions_to_ask: Do I know this client well enough as a person — their goals, their pressures, their family situation — that they would describe me as a friend, not just a vendor?
When did I last do something for this client that had nothing to do with MOTM's commercial interests?
Am I showing up in person with this client regularly enough to build the kind of relationship depth that expansion conversations require?
recommended_action: Build a personal relationship investment plan for every major MOTM client. This includes: meeting in person at least quarterly, remembering and following up on personal milestones, doing at least one thing per quarter that demonstrates investment in the client's success beyond the project scope, and growing the circle of friends within the client beyond the primary buyer.
what_not_to_do: Do not treat client relationships as transactional until the renewal approaches. Do not communicate with clients only when there is a project milestone or a commercial reason. Do not underestimate the competitive advantage of being the person a client genuinely likes and trusts as a human being — in expert services, this is often the deciding factor.
motm_application: A MOTM BD person who has a strong personal relationship with a client's Sales Head will be the first call when the MD is looking for additional sales support in a new market. A MOTM BD person who only communicates when there is a project update will be one of several vendors evaluated when the opportunity arises. The personal relationship investment is not soft — it is a direct commercial driver.

principle_name: Discipline 3 — Leverage Your Team: Grow the Client Relationship Through Careful Introduction of Colleagues
author: Tom McMakin & Jacob Parks
when_to_use: When the natural expansion of a MOTM engagement requires introducing a different capability or a different person into the client relationship. This is how EXPAND, EXTEND, and REACH work happens.
when_not_to_use: Do not introduce a colleague into a client relationship before the original trust and credibility have been firmly established. Do not rush colleague introductions before you know the colleague well enough to stake your own credibility on their work quality.
principle: The exponential growth of any expert services firm within a client comes from the firm acting as a team — not from a single expert deepening one relationship indefinitely. Thierry Chassaing of BCG explains: You cannot see all the opportunities to bring value to a client. Others in your firm will bring their perspective and plant their own flags, which drives exponential growth. But colleague introductions are fraught with risk: the client does not know the new person, the original expert risks losing account control, and the new expert must rebuild trust and credibility from a lower starting point. The best practitioners vet colleagues before introducing them, are present during the initial introduction, and frame it explicitly as adding value rather than handing off responsibility.
questions_to_ask: Who in the MOTM team has a capability that would be valuable to this client — and do I know them well enough to stake my credibility on their work?
What is the specific framing of this colleague introduction that makes it feel like an addition of value to the client rather than a hand-off?
How do I stay connected to this client relationship after introducing a colleague, so the trust I have built continues to support the expansion?
recommended_action: Before any colleague introduction, spend time with the colleague to understand their specific expertise and vetting their approach. Frame the introduction to the client explicitly as bringing additional expertise to serve a specific need the client has expressed — not as transferring the account. Be present at the first meeting between the colleague and the client to facilitate trust transfer.
what_not_to_do: Do not introduce a colleague you do not know personally well enough to vouch for. Do not do a bait-and-switch — winning work based on one person's credibility and then delivering through a different person. Do not disappear from the relationship after introducing a colleague — the original relationship is the anchor that makes the expansion possible.
motm_application: When MOTM's account relationship is with a Sales Head and an opportunity arises to introduce MOTM's capability to the Operations Head, the BD person should: meet with the MOTM person who will lead that conversation before the introduction, ask the Sales Head for a specific warm introduction with a brief explanation of why the Operations Head would benefit, attend the first meeting between MOTM and the Operations Head, and stay connected to both relationships.

principle_name: Discipline 5 — Listen: The Single Most Important BD Skill in Expert Services Is Genuine Listening
author: Tom McMakin & Jacob Parks
when_to_use: In every client and prospect interaction. Listening is not a technique to deploy selectively — it is the continuous practice that reveals where help is needed and when the timing is right.
when_not_to_use: Listening does not mean passive engagement. It must be accompanied by smart, specific questions that demonstrate genuine understanding and expertise. Listening without incisive questions is just silence.
principle: Professor Christopher Stevens at Gonzaga Business School identifies listening as the single skill most important in business — and the one most neglected. Expert services providers are trained to be experts — to give answers, demonstrate knowledge, and impress with insight. But the greatest BD professionals in expert services ask more questions than they answer. By asking smart, specific questions — not generic brochure questions but questions that demonstrate genuine understanding of the client's situation — they signal that they are there to help, not to sell. And through listening, they hear the unmet needs, the political dynamics, the upcoming budget decisions, and the emerging problems that represent the next wave of opportunity. The CEO who raved about a consultant said not because they provided answers but because they came to ask questions whether selling or not.
questions_to_ask: What are your three biggest priorities for this year — and how is your current sales execution aligned with those priorities?
What is the one thing in your sales process that keeps you up at night?
If you could change one thing about how your team is developing new accounts, what would it be?
recommended_action: Build a listening practice into every MOTM client interaction. Before every client meeting, prepare three specific questions that demonstrate genuine understanding of that client's specific situation — not generic questions about their industry. After every client meeting, document the answers and identify any unmet needs or emerging opportunities that emerged. Share observations proactively — do not wait for the client to ask.
what_not_to_do: Do not open client meetings with a presentation or a capability overview before listening. Do not ask generic questions that any consultant could ask without specific knowledge of the client. Do not listen only when you sense a commercial opportunity — listen continuously, because opportunities emerge unexpectedly from genuine conversations.
motm_application: A MOTM BD person visiting an existing client should arrive with three specific questions prepared about what they have observed in the current engagement — not a presentation about what else MOTM can do. The questions demonstrate that MOTM has been paying attention and thinking about the client's situation. The answers will reveal where the next conversation should go. Dave Lubowe of EY said his client chose him over other consultants because he showed up to ask questions whether he was selling or not.

principle_name: Discipline 7 — Master the Art of the Ask: Eventually You Must Ask Directly for the Work
author: Tom McMakin & Jacob Parks
chapter: Chapter 18 — Discipline 7: Master the Art of the Ask
when_to_use: After delivering excellent work, building a genuine relationship, demonstrating additional capabilities through listening and insight, and identifying a specific opportunity where MOTM can help. All seven disciplines must be in motion before the ask lands effectively.
when_not_to_use: Do not ask before the foundation is in place. An ask that comes without demonstrated value, without a genuine relationship, and without a specific observed need will feel like a sales pitch — and it will be rejected.
principle: All the listening, all the relationship investment, all the excellent work, all the discipline — it must eventually lead to an ask. Expert services professionals who do not ask miss enormous opportunities. The ask in expert services is not I want your business. It is I have noticed something that I think we could help with — and I would like to talk about it. The ask flows naturally from genuine observation and genuine investment in the client's success. It is not a closing technique — it is the natural conclusion of the never-say-sell philosophy. The Ask before the Ask is particularly powerful: getting the client to agree to have a conversation about a specific opportunity before the formal proposal is made. This reduces resistance and ensures the ask is heard in the context of genuine helpfulness.
questions_to_ask: Based on what I have observed, there is something specific I think we could help with — can I share what I am seeing and get your reaction?
We have been talking about X for a few months — is now the right time to explore whether MOTM can help with that?

You mentioned that the biggest challenge you are facing right now is Y — that is exactly the kind of thing we have helped other companies with. Can we have a conversation about what that might look like?
recommended_action: In every major MOTM client relationship, identify the one or two most natural next expansion opportunities based on observation and listening. Make the ask explicitly — not as a formal proposal but as a conversation invitation. Use the Ask before the Ask: first get agreement to explore the opportunity, then develop the proposal. This two-step approach dramatically increases conversion.
what_not_to_do: Do not avoid asking because it feels uncomfortable or because you worry about damaging the relationship. The relationship is damaged far more by never asking than by asking respectfully and specifically. Do not make a general ask like is there anything else we can help with — make a specific ask based on a specific observed need. Do not skip the Ask before the Ask and go straight to a formal proposal — test the water first.
motm_application: When a MOTM BD person has observed that their client's Sales Head is struggling with a specific problem — say, no structured approach to cold calling — the ask should be: I have been watching how your team handles initial outreach and I think there is something specific we could do to improve it. Can I share what I am seeing and we can talk about whether it makes sense for us to help? This is the ask in never-say-sell language — specific, observation-based, and framed as a conversation rather than a pitch.

principle_name: Know Thy Client — Deep Understanding of the Client's Situation Creates Natural Expansion Opportunities
author: Tom McMakin & Jacob Parks
when_to_use: Continuously throughout every active MOTM client engagement. Deep knowledge of the client's strategic intent, budget cycle, political dynamics, and emerging priorities is what creates genuine expansion conversations rather than opportunistic pitches.
when_not_to_use: This is not a reason to conduct intrusive research or to access confidential information inappropriately. All client knowledge should be gathered through open, transparent conversations and publicly available information.
principle: Every rainmaker interviewed reported that deep study of the client's situation was the foundation of their ability to grow accounts. Will Williams of KPMG: You've got to be a deep, deep student of the client and understand the business challenges they face. Dave Lubowe of EY goes to clients and says: Based on our understanding of your company, we think you might be interested in this point of view — and then he opens the aperture. His approach communicates three things simultaneously: I care enough about you to have thought about this, I have thought specifically about your business, and I am not selling — I am sharing an observation and leaving the choice with you. This is the never-say-sell approach at its most sophisticated.
questions_to_ask: What is driving the company's overall strategy this year — and how does our current engagement connect to that?
When does this client's budget cycle begin — and are we positioned to have input before the budget is set?
What are the political dynamics in this client organisation that could affect our ability to expand the relationship — and are we navigating them wisely?
recommended_action: Build a structured account intelligence practice for every major MOTM client. This includes: staying alert to public news about the client, understanding the budget cycle and being present at the right moments, understanding the political dynamics between key buyers, and attending internal events where possible. Bring at least one new specific insight to every client meeting — something that demonstrates MOTM has been thinking about the client's situation between meetings.
what_not_to_do: Do not show up to client meetings with only project status to discuss. Do not pitch services to a client without specific knowledge of their current strategic priorities. Do not send generic thought leadership to clients — send specific observations about their situation. Do not miss the budget cycle — if MOTM is not part of the conversation when the budget is being set, they will not be in the budget.
motm_application: A MOTM BD person who knows that their client is planning a market expansion in Q3 can proactively say: We have seen this before with other clients expanding into new markets — the sales execution challenge is usually about territory coverage and account prioritisation. We have some specific experience with this. Would it be useful to talk about what we have seen work? This observation demonstrates deep knowledge, creates a natural expansion conversation, and positions MOTM as a strategic partner rather than a vendor.

principle_name: The Power of Peers — Use Peer Credibility and Introductions to Accelerate Trust in New Buyers
author: Tom McMakin & Jacob Parks
when_to_use: When attempting to reach a new buyer within an existing client organisation, or when trying to establish credibility with a senior prospect who does not yet know MOTM's work.
when_not_to_use: Peer referrals only work if the peer's relationship with the new buyer is genuinely positive. A forced or lukewarm peer referral can be worse than no referral at all.
principle: Trust and credibility travel fastest through peer networks. When a senior executive hears about MOTM from a peer they respect — not from a vendor — the credibility transfer is dramatically faster and more powerful than any amount of direct BD effort. The most effective way to reach a new buyer within a client organisation or a senior prospect outside it is through a warm peer introduction. This is not manipulation — it is how expert services have always been bought: on reputation, referral, and relationship. Building a deliberate peer network strategy — identifying who the right peers are and investing in those relationships proactively — is one of the highest-leverage BD activities available.
questions_to_ask: Which of our existing clients' senior leaders would be the most credible peer reference for the new buyer we are trying to reach?
What would need to be true for our existing client to be willing and enthusiastic about introducing us to their peer in another organisation?
How can we make it easy for our clients to refer us — by giving them a specific story to tell, a specific outcome to cite?
recommended_action: For every major account expansion or new prospect target, identify the ideal peer reference — a senior executive who has experienced MOTM's work and would be enthusiastic about introducing MOTM to a peer. Invest in making that reference person's experience exceptional. Then ask specifically and explicitly for the introduction — not a general endorsement but a specific warm introduction to the named person.
what_not_to_do: Do not ask for referrals from clients who have only had a satisfactory experience — the referral will be lukewarm and will damage rather than build credibility. Do not ask for general referrals — ask for a specific introduction to a specific named person. Do not rely only on direct BD for reaching new senior buyers — peer referrals are dramatically more effective.
motm_application: When MOTM is trying to reach the MD of a new prospect company, the most effective path is through a peer introduction from an MD who has worked with MOTM and had an excellent experience. The BD person should identify who in MOTM's existing client base knows the target MD, invest in making their experience exceptional, and then ask specifically: Do you know [MD Name] at [Company]? Would you be willing to introduce us? We have done something for your business that I think would be relevant to a challenge they are facing.
